This paper investigates convergence for discretization methods in stochastic control problems involving rough path data. Additionally, the text applies these results to an uncoupled zero-mean robust filtering problem for a fully coupled model, ensuring the paper's methodology yields a method to approximately resolve this challenging robust filtering system.

The formation of the quark-glom plasma (QGP), the QCD medium with remarkable characteristics, is confirmed through the analysis of numerous observables in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Recent findings from the ALICE collaboration in LHC proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions demonstrate significant enhancements in event-by-event fluctuations for various hadrons compared to proton-proton data. This study investigates the nature of these fluctuations within a small-system context by presenting an examination of toy-model calculations alongside updated single-photon and non-abelian parton-hadron scattering results from the JANUS collaboration. We focus on whether such increased heterogeneity arises from initial or final states by comparing small and large system data. While increased initial-state complexity due to geometry or fluctuations can account for these effects in small systems, non-abelian final-state interactions also play a crucial non-abelian role in generating similar levels of variability even for small systems. We further explore whether specific hadron types exhibit increased fluctuation on the right path to generate such results, potentially serving as a probe of QGP properties.

Consistent querying represents a critical and growing area of research in databases, concentrating on formulating and assessing queries against databases adhering to specific assumptions regarding functional and equational dependencies. Traditionally, consistent query evaluation has been addressed through polynomial-time algorithms based on the interval logic $\mathbb{R}[X; \mid\cdot|\,, \max, \min, \{0,1\}_x]$, which manages absolute values but restricted operations on minima and maxima. This study presents a comprehensive framework of interval logic $\mathbb{R}[X; \mid\cdot|\,, \max, \min, \{0,1\}_x]$ to establish consistency as a decision problem within P-time relative to a complete four-valued logic $L_4$. Notably, $\{0,1\}_x$ designates bit values for boolean truth given by bit logic $\mathbb{R}[X; \mid\cdot|\,, \max, \min]$. The framework extends previous systems by incorporating relative operations on maxima and minima alongside bit operations, enabling more intricate rule sets while retaining consistent performance. Consequently, the author demonstrates that this expanded logic preserves consistent query evaluation capabilities.

We introduce the novel Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, designed to simultaneously capture nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks in both the level and slope of Poisson series while accommodating time-dependent relationships between and among processes as well as evolving external variables. Under broad assumptions regarding parameter drift and covovariation, we establish the scale dependence of the associated random walk approximations and derive functional random walk and continuous time Poisson approximations as convergence tools. The model's key features allow it to handle scenarios generating continuous time Poisson movements, full coherence in covariance structures, and integrated superdiffusion phenomena. The paper begins by defining the TV-PARX framework and presenting associated theorems that ensure the validity of these approximation methods and their implications for moment and covovariation stability. Subsequent sections cover the analysis of regression relationships and the study of endogeneity effects within this model, with the concluding chapter dedicated to the computation of maximum likelihood estimates and their asymptotic properties under the new framework.

It is demonstrated that under a specific regime of easy peeling, rapid TAP free energy convergence ensures rapid convergence of the AMP algorithm itself. Conversely, the difficult peeling regime is characterized by a second phase transition linked to a replica symmetry breaking transition in the TAP equations; however, in this context, a directed semi-TAP formulation is employed to demonstrate that the APT equations converge in polynomial time without reaching high accuracy. Furthermore, it is established that the APT equations fail to exist in the easy peeling region, yet they remain consistent with the analysis of simple majority voting in the difficult peeling region. Finally, various analytical results regarding the phase transitions observed in this $\text{Z}_2}$-synchronization system are derived and shared.

Wide-field photometry serves as an economical method for monitoring air quality, yet it typically demands expensive on-site radiometric calibration to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD). This study demonstrates that such direct calibration is unnecessary; instead, relative AOD (rAOD) can be used to track AOD variability with high accuracy. The authors propose a straightforward algorithm to calculate rAOD relative to a reference station's vertical rAOD of 1.0. Testing this method involved data from two universities' installed SunSkypix instruments across diverse terrains, including one site near the reference station. The algorithm showed strong agreement with both the standard instrument configuration and AERONET datasets. Object pose estimation is a critical capability for robots operating in real-world scenarios, yet it remains highly challenging due to occlusions, viewpoint variations, and occluded or unfamiliar parts. To address these issues, we propose a pose estimation approach for single images that leverages the inherent geometric constraints of litters, specifically projection grouping and the alignment between world and image coordinate projections. Our framework first groups detected object part hypotheses based on whether their projected geometries are mutually consistent. These groups subsequently serve as input for a support vector regression (SVR) model trained to generate a support score indicating how well each hypothesis aligns with camera extrinsic parameters. Evaluations conducted on the LINEMOD and our self-developed LiteG dataset demonstrate that this proposed grouping support score outperforms traditional methods relying on individual hypothesis support scores. Furthermore, our approach exhibits a distinct advantage over state-of-the-art learning-based techniques, particularly when compared to methods like DeepReinforce, which demand significant training time and extensive computational resources.

Comparing the computational cost and accuracy of different numerical methods is critical for biomolecular simulations, where constraints often arise from both physical and numerical sources. To evaluate various integration algorithms used with both fixed and fluctuating numerical heat baths, this study focuses on the Alanine dipeptide under fixed numerical conditions, employing: (i) the harmonic oscillator coupled to a Debye bath (which mimics a protein's high-frequency modes) and (ii) a pure harmonic bath (representing its low-frequency modes). Using alanine dipeptide data, we compared methods including the BAOAB variant (derived via Baos for constant-temperature simulation with a fixed numerical heat bath) alongside standard algorithms such as Verlet, BBK, and SVDD, applied with both numerical heat baths. Our results indicate that BA0AB achieves the most accurate sampling of the correct statistical distribution while maintaining the lowest computational cost, followed closely by standard Verlet. However, when utilizing a fixed numerical heat bath, both BA0AB and standard Verlet exhibit slight systematic errors in sampling that diminish as the time step decreases. Furthermore, we observe that standard Verlet and the original BAOAB methods yield nearly identical outcomes when implemented with a fluctuating heat bath.

Multilayer networks are characterized by the significant role of inter-layer connections, yet most assessment methods for node importance either disregard these constraints or rely on simplified assumptions. This often results in assessment models that do not align with the actual characteristics of multilayer networks. In this study, we introduce a significance framework based on an individual-node approach. By applying various patterns of inter-layer limitations, we develop a general algorithm to calculate node importance. Subsequently, we extend this approach to determine the criticality of inter-layer links and demonstrate how modifying their own importance influences adjacent nodes. Finally, we validate our proposed model against an established importance measure for multilayer networks and successfully apply it to analyze the structure of air routes.

This study investigates the effects of impact velocities on surface seal performance. As the impact speed increases, the water-air cavity expands due to a drop in internal pressure, increasing the exposed surface area and thus elevating corrosion risks and corrosion rates. The hydrodynamic characteristics were analyzed through both computational fluid dynamics and experimental methods to examine the seal's behavior across different water-air cavity depths. Results indicate that adjusting the bottom arc radius allows for increased pressure, which decreases the smooth surface area subjected to water air-cavity effects.

The long-standing mystery regarding the thermodynamic stability range and inclusive magnetic order of Ni$_3$S$_2$ (cubanite) finds its resolution in the present study through first-principles calculations. It becomes evident that Ni$_3$S$_2$ exhibits nearly flat-band behavior in its lowest energy states, a characteristic directly responsible for both its heightened stability threshold and ferromagnetic alignment. Specifically, first-principles methods reveal that the stability limit of Ni$_3$S$_2$ shifts toward more reduced chemical potentialities as on-site repulsion ($U$) increases, concomitantly strengthening ferromagnetic tendency; however, these effects only manifest when the value of $U$ surpasses approximately 1.5 eV.

In our analysis, we demonstrate through explicit examples of various coherent state families, each catalyzed by a solitary photon, how their availability for use—as indicated by success rates—is impacted differently depending on whether the one-phoni catalysis achieved through a beam splitter or a parametric device. Through explicit state comparisons, we illustrate the specific source of variability in the measure of classical behavior, and identify the root origin for changes in the probability of a successful interaction.

Long-standing theoretical inquiries into the thermodynamics and kinetic dynamics of macromolecules now face a critical challenge: accurately modeling a specific monomer's interactions with other monomers to predict polymers' macroscopic behavior. While standard molecular dynamics and coarse-grained simulations offer potential solutions, these methods often require extensive computational resources and still struggle to maintain accuracy. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a data-driven approach utilizing a deep neural network to determine the free energy landscape and general forces acting on each monomer, based solely on pairwise distances with the rest of the monomer chain. This method formulates the problem as a dynamic process where the neutral monomer seeks its equilibrium shape by minimizing a potential energy surface derived from the learned forces. Our framework has been validated through multiple scenarios, including all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of an all-trans polyethylene segment, demonstrating its ability to accurately replicate monomeric forces, structural characteristics, and thermodynamic properties across varying temperatures. By training the model on data generated from standard molecular dynamics, this inference approach provides a significantly more computationally efficient pathway to reliably simulate the dynamics and behavior of specific polymers defined by their monomeric composition.

This work introduces a new deep learning architecture, the Dilated Dense Attention Unet (D2A-Net), specifically designed to enhance the automatic segmentation of esophageal tumors in CT images. The architecture aims to extract features across diverse spatial scales to enhance boundary delineation while minimizing interference from irrelevant regions. The network integrates multiple archimedean unets (I) at varying dilated attention rates to progressively capture both local and global features. The corresponding segmentations are then fused using a mechanism that applies undilated attention to the lower unites for refinement. The undilated unites utilize the input image directly, facilitating more accurate segmentation of small structures. To evaluate the model, we used the recently released End Cancer Unites dataset, which was not accessible during the initial D2A unites release. The proposed approach was systematically compared against prominent existing approaches. The quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that the unites dilated attention (I) architecture significantly improves the precision and consistency of unites tumor segmentation in unites esophageal CT images.

While online interaction was once thought to effectively bridge geographical divides, the reverse often holds true, a phenomenon known as "The Big Sort." In this context, individuals in segregated communities—whether due to political leanings or other factors—frequently share the same views and circulate similar content online. Relying on a new dataset that maps the regional origins of U.S. Facebook users, we demonstrate that misinformation regarding COVID-Vaxx cards experienced distinct peaks in geographically segmented groups, indicating that "The Big Sort" operates significantly within Facebook ecosystems as well.

In this study, we investigate the variability of speech data within simulation environments, specifically examining Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) policies trained across different demonstration frequencies and task difficulties. By exploring variations in task complexity and training data diversity, we analyze how these elements influence the semantic content of an student agent's utterances. Research reveals that increased task difficulty and low demonstration frequencies result in more intricate speech patterns containing additional semantic concepts, even when those concepts were not present during training. Furthermore, we analyze the RNN internal structures to understand the linguistic composition of the student agent's output. Building on the discovery that difficult tasks produce speech with unfamiliar, non-trained concepts, we developed a hypothesis regarding the mechanism behind this phenomenon, testing it through simulations that manipulated task difficulty. These new simulations provided support for the initial hypothesis, indicating that increased difficulty prompts the student agent to internalize and reproduce concepts that are not immediately useful for completing the specific task. Additionally, we explored the effect of heterogeneity in training data, specifically by analyzing speech data variability caused by changes in demonstration styles, verbal guidance content, intermediate task steps, and system mistakes. The results indicate that specific features such as inaccurate demonstrations or complex audio instructions directly correlate with increased variability in the speech produced by the learned policy.

Rapid advancements in automated testing frameworks are essential to bring conversational systems to market. Nevertheless, crafting effective tests remains arduous due to the vast and varied landscape of self-driving frameworks designed to navigate dialogue flows. This study introduces a new self-driving testing framework specifically optimized for customer service chatbots. We present the first systematic comparison of these methodologies within a genuine customer service context. The authors built two large-scale real-world driving tests, each encompassing over 1,000 dialogue turns, to manage user journeys through new chatbot deployments in the customer service sector. The study introduces a self-driving testing dataset and evaluation benchmark tailored to this domain. The framework proposed by the study significantly lowers the barrier for creating self-driving tests in non-game contexts and offers a strict metric for comparing self-driving performance specifically within customer service chatbot interactions.

In today's rapidly evolving internet era, recommendation systems have become indispensable within user interfaces across various platforms to streamline content discovery and enhance the overall experience. Within these recommendation frameworks, sidecars—specifically comments—are increasingly utilized to surface user preferences; however, existing literature largely overlooks the dynamic evolution of user preferences when learning from such feedback. To address this gap, we introduce a novel framework known as Dynamic Sidecar-based Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE), which aims to improve user preference learning by integrating comment aspect terminology with corresponding feedback. Furthermore, to effectively capture the nuanced preferences expressed in comments, we develop an attention mechanism that prioritizes facet-specific sentiment, employing pairwise interactions within a graph-based neural network structure. By combining these aspect-based enhancements with gated preference evolution, our approach enables more precise modeling of how user preferences change over time. We validate the proposed method through extensive experiments on two real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and providing significant insights.

We assess seven deep learning models trained on partially overlapping subsets of the large OASIS-1 dataset to analyze how specific data compositions influence performance on completely unseen MRI scans. Results, measured using Categorical Cross-Enents (CCC) for continuous values and show that performance varies significantly depending on the specific mix of content within each subset. This confirms that despite the scale of the OASIS dataset, certain subclasses of completely new, high-quality images can yield superior outcomes compared to larger, alternative subsets of completely new, diverse images. We introduce a framework for network-based multi-agent optimization (MBO), which encompasses a wide range of existing multi-agent models by defining it through a graph where nodes represent individual agents and edges denote interactions or constraints. To enable efficient distributed solutions, we propose a general dual decomposition (DD) strategy, characterizing the local residual errors introduced by dual relaxation as consistency costs. Agents situated directly connected via edges have access to impose these costs to guide peers in converging toward dual optimality. Within this setting, each agent manages a local subproblem and interacts solely with neighbors to execute the algorithm's steps. We evaluate two specific algorithms featuring differing local update mechanisms and prove the convergence of their iterates and costs, ensuring that any limit point yields an optimal dual solution. Subsequently, we demonstrate how this general framework and the derived algorithms apply to solve two key instances: a previously studied MBO variant utilizing specific consistency costs and a decentralized machine learning model relying on dual constraints with similar structures. Numerical experiments using the dual updating rule from the first optimization case validate the proposed methods and the dual updating approach across multiple agents and various dimensions of the MBO problem.

We introduce a novel multi-agent framework based on the Motivation Dynamics (MOTIF) that analyzes how autonomous vehicles navigate around each other during a rendezvous. This extension defines a set of motivations, adapted specifically for this interaction, where each vehicle makes movement decisions by evaluating pairwise differential motional patterns between the pair. Our primary contribution to the existing framework is the definition of these vehicle-specific motivations and their application in mutual approach navigation. To our knowledge, this particular multi-agent configuration within MOTIF has not been explored before. Through simulation-based experiments, we demonstrate the framework's effectiveness and validate that each agent can independently choose a motivation to facilitate a successful meeting point selection and approach behavior.

The crystal electric field (CEF) energy levels and associated magnetic moments were assessed for Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ across all compositions using $4$-neutron magnetic susceptibility and specific heat measurements at both low and reduced temperatures. The findings indicate that the CEF ground state for pure CmSn$_3$ features a $|^{2}_{2}A_{2}^{2}|\) projection on the principal axis and a characteristic temperature scale of 1.6 K, implying characteristic temperature scale of 1.6 K. In Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the interactions between two heavy quarks are described by a potential, a framework that predicts the masses associated with meson states containing a pair of heavy quarks. This work presents a formal definition of the perturbative expansion for the inter-quark potential within N=4 Super Yang-Mills (SYM) theory using the on-shell formalism. By presenting the results entirely through scattering amplitudes, this approach circumvents many complexities inherent in traditional calculations based on the lattice or path integral methods. Consequently, it enables the computation of the potential via leading-order contributions already at two loops, whereas similar computations using conventional perturbative methods were restricted to just one loop due to higher-order complications. While N=4 SYM serves theoretically as an exact dual counterpart to string theory via the AdS/CFT correspondence, this study re-examines the problem specifically as a perturbative QCD issue utilizing the most direct current. Extending beyond N=4 SYM, this expanded approach becomes feasible at the two-loop level for both the three-heavy-quark configuration and configurations involving at least one light quark pair.

T centre ensembles in carbons-doped silicon exhibit strong spin-photon coupling and otherwise favorable properties for use in quantum technology. Nevertheless, their spin transition optical spectra typically display a mid-gap defect state that evolves over time, causing optical diffusion. This study demonstrates the application of machine learning to characterize the feature-rich data resulting from scanning, spectroscopy, and single-photon counting across individual T centres. By analyzing single-centre dynamics, we find that the previously reported long-term spectral diffusion stems from nearby other carbon impurities. Furthermore, we show that precise single-centre tuning is achievable through localized thermal heating and magnetic field adjustments. These advancements enhance single-centre performance, thereby facilitating more effective quantum communication via fibre and at chip interfaces.

We evaluate the performance of twelve object detectors from leading deep learning frameworks across various tasks within robot manipulation. Additionally, we analyze how the specific use case influences the optimal decision: while factors like data need and latency dictate the final selection in highly constrained or research scenarios, our findings suggest that for standard object detection applications on modern robotic systems, the specific choice of detector is less critical, provided the chosen model meets the necessary latency thresholds and the available training requirements are satisfied.

Kidney transplantation remains limited by a shortage of compatible donors, necessitating that medical teams strategically decide whether to immediately accept an offered kidney or wait for a better match. This study focuses on the policy of "informed waiting," where candidates under monitoring for suitable organs assess each incoming offer and choose either to transplant or to decline. We model this informed waiting process as a stochastic dynamic programming problem, specifically an infinite-horizon Markov Decision Process (MDP) with random timing for transplantation. A core element of this PMP model is treating incompatibility as a state variable; within an MDP framework with a vast action and value function, this variable functions as the most significant distinguishing feature. By analyzing the simplified two-variable case—where a single potential donor type exists with a fixed availability rate—we derive exact solutions. Furthermore, we provide an approximation method involving a finite set of donor types, for which we demonstrate the convergence of approximate value iteration. Finally, decision rules are identified for specific subsets of the problem, and these are utilized to verify properties of the overall policy across the general model structure.

The result is a new dataset containing over 1,000 curated English-Financial term pairs that include both antonyms and their corresponding translations in sentiment opposite forms across six other languages (e.g., German, French, Spanish, etc.). In the increasingly competitive mobile markets, the simultaneous advancement of throughput, fair-throughput, and novel communication-sensing tradeoffs within wideband waveforming strategies is becoming both a significant challenge and an opportunity. Addressing this, we propose a unified framework designed to maximize either fair or total throughput while maintaining minimum guaranteed throughputs for specific subcarriers, subject to constraints on fair or total energy steering radar (ESTR) performance. By formulating these objectives as non-convex optimization problems, we develop efficient solution approaches based on successive convex approximation and geometric methods. Key innovations include a novel technique for transforming the fair-throughput metric and a new convex relaxation of the feasibility region derived from ESTR constraints. These innovations facilitate a significant reduction in the original complex optimization task into simpler sub-problems that can be solved efficiently. Extensive numerical simulations confirm the validity of our theoretical results and demonstrate the superiority of the proposed optimization framework over conventional designs.

This study proposes a novel approach utilizing a conventional neural network (CNN) to model the complex nonlinear dynamics characterizing Rayleigh-Bénard instability in fluid dynamics. The primary objective involves forecasting the time-evolving velocity and temperature fields given initial conditions and specific system parameters such as the Rayleigh number. To achieve this, we formulated a variational loss function incorporating a novel architecture designed for resolution upscaling, enabling accurate future field prediction from low-resolution representations learned from high-resolution input data. Additionally, the research presents a qualitative analysis leveraging our network to reveal the underlying coherent structures within this nonlinear system.

We investigate first-passage stochastic games where both members of a duopoly seek to learn Nash equilibriums. We introduce a combination of two methods: CO, an application of the Optimistic H4 algorithm tailored for duopolists, and V, an adaptation of the Iterated Optimistic B4 algorithm specifically for this duopoly setting. We analyze the relationship between the strategies emerging from our proposed "Optimistic H4 vs. Optimistic H4" learning process and those from the "Iterated Optimistic H4 vs. Iterated Optimistic H4" process. Specifically, we demonstrate that if one agent employs CO while the other uses V, it guarantees that any action iteratively dominated relative to CO's learned behavior will be avoided with high probability by the using CO, provided it is also acted upon iteratively to approach equilibrium. This result holds true when CO is applied iteratively as well. These theoretical findings are substantiated through experiments in various scenarios involving square and rectangular ground areas of differing dimensions, comparing CO in action against V, and also comparing CO's iterative use against itself.

This study introduces and examines an epidemic model featuring dynamic contact networks and rewiring mechanisms, where infection spreads via probabilistic transmission upon contact, and contact patterns evolve through deterministic matching and rewiring processes. Our primary finding demonstrates that if rewiring increases contacts beyond the stability threshold, the final infection fraction rises to nearly one regardless of initial network structure or initial infection levels. Furthermore, when contacts decrease below this threshold, the final infection load depends heavily on the initial configuration, particularly regarding its proximity to the critical value. Subsequent analysis provides an explicit formula for this critical contact level and includes simulation results to validate these theoretical predictions.

We investigate a scenario in which ultralight dark matter interacts with neutrinos through a dark Higgs force that remains active before electroweak symmetry breaking. This coupling disrupts the cosmic evolution of the infant universe by dark matter-neutrum scattering and by modifying the dynamics of the weak transition and early expansion. A new nonlocal non-Abelian constitutive relation is introduced, which links the field strength tensor to measurable quantities via a nonlocal operator acting upon the dual field strength tensor. This nonlocal framework yields gravitational theories that align with local Einstein gravity while preserving the full nonlinearity characteristic of non-Abian gravity. Consequently, the vacuum field equations take a form identical to Einstein's, with coupling determined by a specific combination of nonlocal operators and a single real parameter. However, when matter is involved, the situation diverges significantly from both Einstein-Maxwell and Einstein-Dirac formulations. Instead, the resulting framework resembles Einstein-Higgs, yet without spontaneous symmetry breaking. This leads to long-range interactions mediated by massive vector bosons, whose ranges increase with growing nonlocal non-Abianity and extend to infinity even when the parameter is vanishingly small. Furthermore, the model allows for the construction of black holes, where the traditional event horizon is replaced by a region of extremely high curvature. Such a substitute, distinct from a singularity, could potentially offer a viable route to exploring quantum gravity effects.

The detection of a significant number of neutron stars obscured as low-luminosity X-ray sources is anticipated across various domains, with the Galaxy's millisecond radio pulsars representing a prominent example. However, the mechanisms enabling the transition from radio state to high H α recombination emission in low-intensity millisecond sources have proven elusive to date. We argue that the population of low-active X-ray sources known as Neutron Star Low-Mass X-Ray Binaries (NS-LMBs)—which remain undetectable when inactive—represents the most viable solution. These sources align closely with millisecond pulsars regarding spin periods, spectral characteristics, and, crucially, the propensity for high H α emission when quiescent. Furthermore, the calculated number of NS-LMBs in the NS-LMB model is consistent with the count of low-luminosity millisecond radio pulsars, while also offering testable forecasts for upcoming observational campaigns designed to identify such sources.

The traditional concept of tuning reaction rate constants in barrier exothermic reactions through the coupling of vibrational modes to quantum states in free energy has been identified as a barrier-raising mechanism. This coupling, whether induced by structured environments or specific interfaces, can simultaneously lower both the enthalpy and the fundamental activation barrier of barrier exothermic reactions. Consequently, reaction rate constants might be controlled more effectively when the barrier itself is modified, not just the thermal component of the rate. Furthermore, this barrier-exothermicity coupling influences the sensitivity of these reactions to temperature changes. We examine the implications of this phenomenon for relevant systems, such as the water self-ionization process and enzymatic reactions like lysozyme acting on crystalline substrates versus its transition states, and potential water self-ionization processes.

Dialogue generation often suffers from limited output diversity, which hinders widespread real-world use. While various strategies exist to increase this diversity, most are ineffective. We identify the root cause of this lack of variety as a low-diversity latent space produced by current non-linear models. Building on this insight, we propose a framework that increases diversity in dialogue responses directly during generation without requiring retraining. Specifically, we introduce a mechanism that samples a diversity-increasing signal from noise and integrates it via a new attention module designed to promote variety. Experiments on two standard dialog datasets demonstrate that our approach effectively enhances diversity while maintaining high semantic similarity between dialogue turns and other essential dialogue characteristics.

It has long been established that every planar bipartite graph can be drawn planarly where edges are straight lines, as proven by Stein and Wagner in 1997 using the strategy of refining a given refinement by splitting vertices to apply their 1994 result for trees. While this method was feasible for small numbers of refinements or simple graphs, it becomes unviable for large unrefined graphs due to the exponential growth in size when splitting. In this paper, we present an improved approach that coarsely divides Stein and Wagner's refinement into two distinct parts: a middle planar structure known as a "dumbell" and a refined middle graph called a "tree of dumbells." We then demonstrate how to merge these components to achieve a straight-line planar depiction of the original graph, effectively resolving it into a valid graph drawing.

Bipedal walking models represent the most advanced self-locomotion technique for bipedal robots, yet integrating control strategies with sufficient robustness and efficacy remains a significant challenge. Implementing closed-loop feedback is essential to handle both internal and external disturbances throughout a gait; however, traditional methods often rely on computationally demanding trajectory optimizations or complex feedback laws. In contrast, this study proposes a streamlined approach for generating closed-loop feedback that does not require heavy computation. The method involves injecting measured state errors into the time symmetric trajectory, which serves as the initial symmetric pattern for an optimization process. Results demonstrate that this proposed method successfully achieves robust, time-symmetric walks capable of responding to feedback even when significant deviations occur or when the target trajectory differs from that of open-loop optimization.

Flush+Reload is the leading method for estimating the lifespan of CPU side-channel vulnerabilities. Although powerful, the technique's practical success is hindered by the overheads of hyperthreading flushing and redirect streams. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a flush and redirect strategy specifically engineered for non-hyperthreading contexts that achieves a twofold reduction in attack implementation costs. Furthermore, the method enhances attack precision by achieving micro-op level time granularity. As demonstrated through experiments on Intel Xeon Gold 6230 processors, results indicate a 30% decrease in required system calls and a threefold increase in flush and reload signal variance compared to current standards. The authors also present FlushTrack, a novel algorithm utilizing variance analysis to identify exact match tracks among candidates. Experiments confirm this capability reduces flush and reload overhead by 14% with added implementation complexity. Combining HyperDegrade and FlushTrack yields a significant 40% reduction in the trace count required for the attack, alongside the successful identification of side-channel traces with zero hyperthreading interference. These contributions collectively establish a more effective Flush+Reload framework, facilitating side-channel exploitation at finer time scales and higher signal clarity.

This study examines decision-making within a multi-agent system dealing with stochastic and dynamic tasks, where each agent selects between automating task execution through collaboration with others or managing it independently. We evaluate how varying task difficulty distributions influence system performance and how adaptive agents respond to these changes. Our findings reveal that system-wide automation rates rise as overall task difficulty increases; however, the impact of individual agent adaptability depends on the nature of the difficulty variation. Specifically, if difficulty increases correlate with an agent's past actions, adaptive adaptability enhances performance. Conversely, if increases stem from external factors like time or random events, an non-adaptive constant strategy for automoting thresholds yields superior outcomes. Furthermore, agents operating under non-adaptive strategies for setting automation thresholds demonstrate robustness against fluctuations in task difficulty.

Regularized kernel regression is widely used for tasks like classification and remains computationally demanding for massive datasets, particularly for the convolution kernel required. Standard approaches to reduce dimensionality while maintaining performance include Random Fourier Features (RFF) and Random Fourier Fourier Features (PRFF). Although PRFFs offer significant dimension reduction, they lack theoretical support for selecting the projection dimension and regularization parameters. This paper investigates two generalized transmission schemes for simultaneous wireless information and power (SWIPT) transmission over integrated networks, utilizing channel statistics to determine optimal power allocation. The first scheme employs direct current (DC) converters to transform harvested oscillating voltages into usable power, featuring a converter model that accounts for efficiency roll-off near transmission frequencies. The paper analyzes two transmission modes: dedicated intervals for either information or power delivery using time-division multiple access (TDMA), and concurrent delivery using orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA). For both the DC converter model and General Antenna-Switching, we formulate an optimization problem aimed at maximizing harvested energy under the constraint that information rates meet a minimum threshold. The resulting optimization for the optimization problem is formulated as maximizing harvested energy under the constraint that information rates are satisfied. The resulting optimization problem for the optimization problem is formulated as maximizing harvested energy under the constraint that information rates are satisfied. The resulting optimization problem is transformed into a form suitable for efficient numerical solution. Numerical results demonstrate the proposed methods, highlighting the effectiveness of the channel estimation-based optimization strategies.

Network robustness regarding sudden attacks or failures has been extensively analyzed. This research investigates the impact of eliminating a node affected by a random failure on the integrity of scale-free networks with different statistical attributes. Our findings indicate that a sufficient magnitude of avalanche—defined as the displaced load from the failed node—is essential to protect the system from breakdown. Furthermore, an avalanche of adequate scale guarantees that the maximum load exceeds the second-highest connectivity threshold within the network, thereby preventing failure irrespective of the specific node removed or the underlying degree distribution. We demonstrate this phenomenon in various models, including the Barabási-Albert preferential attachment network and the Adler-Axelrod-Susmel (AAS) strategy. In the AAS context, we calculate the probability distribution of load transfer required to prevent network collapse and introduce an extended protocol where load follows links with a certain probability.

We introduce the "sloshing-Sagnac" interferometer, a novel configuration that merges the inherent advantages of both Sagnac and Mach-Zehnder types. In this setup, two counter-propagating light beams travel equal distances, yet their paths are arranged to be partially perpendicular rather than parallel. This specific geometry allows for the elimination of certain noise sources present in conventional sloshing (Mach-Zehnder) variants while simultaneously enhancing the signal compared to standard (Sagnac) models. Theoretical analysis employs both the rigorous geometric approach developed by Bertotti and the magnetic-field analogy proposed by Ungar, and experimental findings align closely with these theoretical predictions across diverse configurations. Our work establishes that this new "Bertotti-Ungar" equivalence offers a more robust and general method for understanding beam propagation than earlier, limited theories.

Random access (RA) serves as a critical function in wireless systems, and Next Generation (XL)-Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) systems have aimed to enhance random access (RA) protocols to reach their full potential. However, the proposed schemes still encounter challenges concerning high control plane overhead, elevated probability of collision, and difficulty in managing the data plane. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel, end-to-end network operating vector XL (NOVR-XL) RA protocol tailored for XL-MIMO systems. This approach leverages an over-the-air (OTA) coding method based on an under-sampled orthogonal space multiplexing (OSM) matrix. Such coding enables the simultaneous determination of the control plane and data plane without collision. Simulation results demonstrate that NOVR-XL outperforms existing protocols by offering superior system sustainability, lower protocol overhead, and increased success rates.

Features observed in protoplanetary disks often reveal underlying physical processes, including the growth of embedded planetesimals. While direct evidence from individual disks remains elusive, theoretical models suggest that certain disk structures—such as spirals, vortices, surface density enhancements, and temperature anomalies—can form through interactions between protoplanets and the disk itself. These theoretical mechanisms often reach fragmentation-level masses necessary for efficient planetesimal formation. Conversely, structures too small for traditional hydrodynamic simulations must be investigated using $N$-body methods or hybrid approaches. This work reviews the structures described above, with a specific focus on those capable of forming at sizes limited only by self-gravity. Additionally, it examines structures likely caused by migrating planetesimals interacting with disk gaseous components. Finally, an overview of current observational capabilities and their role in detecting both structures and associated emission signatures is provided.

The BigApple energy density functional (EDF), initially formulated and validated using nuclear matter data and finite nuclear data from various countries, has recently been re-examined specifically through the lens of neutron skin thickness in heavy nuclei. This study details BigApple's foundational structure, its practical applications, and the specific methodologies employed to demonstrate its capabilities in predicting the equation of state of neutron-rich matter. Key focus areas include the functional's handling of incompressibility, neutron proton symmetry energy incompressibility, and related macroscopic properties of nuclear matter. Additionally, the work addresses the model's predictions for several specific neutron-rich nuclei, with particular attention given to 11Li, 39Ar, 111Cd, and 222Th. The paper concludes by exploring BigApple's potential applications in the investigation of extreme astrophysical environments, such as neutron stars.

In this study, we analyze the impact of recently introduced, robust Molmer-Sorensen gates within a trapped-ion architecture, with a specific focus on their capacity to approach unit probability speeds while analyzing entanglement construction in a three-qubit system. By applying a quantitative metric for gate speed, we evaluate various growing strategies employing these fast entanglement tools alongside standard two-qubit variants. Our findings reveal that a growth approach utilizing solely current, robust Molmer-Sorensen gates results in superior outcomes compared to mixed protocols. The proposed growth strategy not only facilitates the rapid development of high-fidelity quantum states but also yields a high-fidelity exponential four-qubit state through the creation of a "Gaussian Greenberger-Horne-Tau" (GGHH). Finally, we address the broader implications of generating high-quality exponential states through repeated applications of such gate mechanisms.

The deployment of storage solutions is crucial for creating resilient, low-carbon electricity markets. Yet, even when storage can technically balance supply and demand, it often remains balanced at zero due to short-term forecasting uncertainties and cost considerations. This study examines how such storage behaviors influence low-carbon policy outcomes by conducting simulations within an agent-based market model featuring risk-averse storage agents under varying carbon tax rates and storage investment costs. Results indicate higher storage capacity utilization—and consequently greater decarbonization and market stability—when storage agents are allowed to self-dispatch based on internal balancing needs rather than being forced to match exact generation output. Furthermore, the findings highlight that both capacity utilization and the effectiveness of carbon pricing are highly sensitive to the level of market risk; specifically, increased risk-aversion diminishes the impact of carbon taxation. Ultimately, these results suggest that future policy designs must explicitly account for storage risk preferences and operational flexibility, suggesting that self-dispatch regulations may require adjustment as storage uncertainty increases.

The current study employs the Whole Atmosphere Mars General Circulation Model (WAMGCM) to investigate baroclinic storms occurring during the intermediate complexity of Martian dust cycles—situated between quiescent intervals and large global heat engine events associated with high solar obliquity. We analyze how these events compare to both typical Martian conditions and Earth-like scenarios. Our findings indicate that the tectonic (or rather, the heat engine) strength in this specific intermediate regime aligns closely with Earth characteristics across various metrics, including the heat engine efficiency coefficient, the Froude number, the Rossby number, and the thermal wind shear magnitude. Consequently, these distinct Martian phenomena appear to be governed primarily by the thermal heat engine rather than radiative processes, yet they adhere to the same scaling laws as the baroclinic instability mechanisms dominant on Earth.

Active learning has long been proven effective, enabling machines to reach levels of human performance with just 10–20 percent labeled data. However, when applied to large-scale image repositories like ImageNet, existing methods struggle due to excessive computational demands and the sparse class distribution inherent in such datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce a scalable active learning approach optimized specifically for image recognition tasks. By integrating an efficient image classifier with heuristic strategies, our method achieves several key improvements over prior art: it calculates the information gain of individual batches to maximize informativeness at scale, utilizes highly performant classifiers to ensure computational efficiency, and incorporates the structural organization of image features to refine selection criteria. Crucially, this approach requires no manual tuning of parameters to adjust the difficulty of selected samples. When evaluated on ImageNet using state-of-the-art classifiers, our method achieves competitive accuracy with actively learned datasets—utilizing only 10 percent of labeled data—demonstrating significant advantages over traditional active learning algorithms in the context of high-volume image environments.

The rapid advancement of machine learning and information technology has led to numerous applications that process and analyze vast amounts of sensitive information, thereby increasing the vulnerability of various organizations and institutions to privacy breaches. Concurrently, differentially private (DP) distributed learning has emerged as a key area of research, offering a robust framework for ensuring privacy in such activities. However, the fundamental interconnectivity of data points within the data structure significantly complicates the computation of privacy loss in DP differential private (DP) settings. Furthermore, the privacy implications of model updates in DP distributed scenarios are difficult to assess, as these depend intricately on the specific distributed architecture employed. Consequently, the broad community of DP distributed learning researchers strives to introduce update formats and distribution strategies that minimize privacy loss while also facilitating private model convergence on robust solutions. However, existing approaches often suffer from overly complex or restrictive assumptions. In contrast, this paper introduces a general and practical methodology for computing robust privacy guarantees regarding different model updates, specifically avoiding strict assumptions about input data. The approach frames the problem as a backward data analysis task that applies forward differential privacy (DP) principles. Our proposed framework has been implemented, tested, and validated within the popular FLlib (Federated Learning library) environment.

Using the Antikaon-64Ni ($\K^-{}^{64}\Ni$) system, a $\K^-$ polarized partial wave analyzer was constructed and deployed within the DA$\Phi$NI facility at GSI to examine the relationship between neutron number and nuclear deformation. This research aimed to trace the evolution of excitation energy for the $3_{2}^{-}$ state in the $64\Ni$ nucleus. This specific energy level serves as a sensitive indicator for changes in the neutron $N=40$ subshell gap and corresponding shifts in the monopole interaction.

To specifically identify the $3_{2}^{-}(3p-2h)$ configuration and suppress contributions from other mixed configurations, the system leveraged the high polarization of incoming $\K^-$ particles and employed linear polarization analysis of scattered $\K^-$ at a center-of-mass angle of $90^\circ$. We propose J-K-fold cross validation (J-KFCV), a novel approach designed to enhance and stabilize performance assessments while enabling effective comparison and ranking of data mining algorithms. Standard K-fold cross validation (KFCV) often exhibits high variance due to the stochastic nature of train-test partitioning; although increasing $K$ can mitigate this variance, it concurrently elevates computational costs. J-KFCV overcomes this challenge by employing multiple independent train-test splits for each of the $K$ folds, where total fold count ensures $(J \times K)$ datasets are generated such that each data point appears in the testing set exactly once. The advantages of J-KFCV include improved stability and variance reduction in performance estimates, streamlined identification and ordering of data mining algorithms, and the benefit of requiring no repetition of experiments, with the trade-off being the increased volume of data points evaluated.

Recent advancements in deep neural networks have sparked a new wave of research focused on lightweight student models designed to achieve the same outputs as more complex teacher architectures. However, these studies often utilize very small dummy inputs for distillation, which limits the model's performance. Addressing this gap, we introduce a novel framework for self-training student networks that leverizes the full outputs—intermediate features included—generated during the self-training process, treating the larger dataset created by training on oneself as an equivalent to a big teacher. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 demonstrate that our student model, though still small, outperforms models trained via traditional single-pass methods, even those "teacher" models used for transfer. Specifically, our approach achieves a student-side speedup in training efficiency by a factor of 30 to 40 compared to single-pass training, and our student model achieves nearly the same results as a single-pass training with a "big teacher" model.

In this study, we introduce rCASPR, a refined linear sampling approach for computational aperture-synthesised radio astronomy (CASPR) sampling. Traditional linear sampling, while effective, introduces aliasing due to its discrete grid layout, degrading both point-spread and overall image quality when paired with linear scan schedules. Although rCASPR employs the same physical movement mechanics, it calculates radio flux through non-uniform, importance-sampling algorithms to avoid these artifacts. We evaluate this method against uniform sampling and other sampling schemes using simulated visibility data processed via the NIFTI pipeline. Results indicate superior performance across the board, with rCASPR specifically outshining traditional linear sampling by enhancing both the clarity of the point-spread function and contrast in final synthesized images. In this study, I construct an ancient "dataset" by estimating historic freight rates between European land locations between 1400 and 1700. These inferences rely on examining historical records of ship cargo holds and comparing them to contemporary grain prices at both origin and destination. By factoring these records through an utility-maximizing framework for merchants, I extract ancient freight rates. Complementary, high-resolution data on grain supply and demand, along with rigorous archival research, reveals that these rates were frequently subject to monopolistic cartels. Such price-fixing arrangements were particularly prevalent during grain scarcity and tight supply conditions, often leading to what modern standards would define as extortionate levels.

The resulting dataset captures the fragmentation of these shipping cartels, an event historians attribute to the actions of the Dutch Republic. The measures introduced by the Dutch influence are observable as significant drops in freight rates and increased cargo volumes. Specifically, the impact of the Dutch breakaway from cartels is evident across a wide area of Europe, with the most pronounced effects seen in the grain trade within the French grain basin.

Using this newly formed dataset on freight rates, I estimate the causal influence of supply and demand, particularly focusing on how grain scarcity and the prevalence of cartels themselves shaped these rates. The primary motivation for creating this ancient dataset is to utilize it as historical background information for analyzing the impact of similar monopolies in the American grain market during the 19th and 20th centuries.

Stock price forecasting holds significant interest for investors seeking to enhance their returns, yet accurate modeling remains challenging due to the strong influence of technical indicators and historical price data. We investigate the correspondence between Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT), specifically examining double Higgs production up to six Higgs bosons. In previous work, we established that the factor of $(N-2)!$ separating the leading terms in HEFT versus SMEFT for $N$ Higgs bosons applies universally to all scattering processes, not just specific production or annihilation events. Specifically, the perturbative expansion in Higgs fields differs between the two formalisms, resulting in a shift of $N$ to the count of Higgs fields. Consequently, the ratio of perturbative expansions for any process involving $n_h$ Higgs fields shifts by $(n_h - 2)!$.

We present a framework for enhancing real-time surface point cloud registration by adapting robust statistical methods for noise reduction. Applications running interpreted languages such as PHP and Python experience a significant performance hit from superfluous system calls generated during the execution of normal business logic. To address this, we introduce Loops, an efficient wall-clock time-based filtering approach that eliminates redundant system calls without requiring white-listing specific calls or instrumenting applications with complex logic. This method has been engineered to handle the nuances of these languages. The resulting runtime performance is so precise that it enables application of the two primary strategies for implementing the time filter. Our evaluation of this tool across a variety of interpreted applications demonstrates its efficacy and accuracy when compared against the current industry standard.

This study introduces an efficient data association approach designed to handle multiple, sparse, and uncorrelated targets within a multiple hypothesis framework. Traditional data association strategies, which rely on matching measurement-to-target and measurement-to-missing data, often impose high computational costs. This burden is especially critical when tracking undetected targets with limited sensor fields of view, as these undetected events occur frequently. The proposed method alleviates this issue by associating clusters of measurements to prediction states of non-detected targets. By reframing the problem, the approach significantly reduces computational requirements. Moreover, it enhances association accuracy among isolated, uncorrelated measurements. Consequently, the system can effectively and precisely track multiple targets, including those missed detections, without compromising performance.

Has there ever a gap in our understanding regarding how the "living" continuum extends beyond binary categories of animate versus inanimate based? We now present the first human crowdsourcing effort to visualize this spectrum from most to least "alive." Our analysis revealed two independent factors influencing one's standing on this continuum: how visibly categorizable an entity is as animate, and its degree of agency. A continuous scale along the continuum effectively captures these dynamics, functioning robustly whether applied to new items within specific categories or across diverse categories when handling new, unseen stimuli. This continuum also outperforms traditional categorical approaches in practical applications, including automated moderation systems and content recommendation algorithms. Finally, we discovered distinct patterns in how humans draw upon visual categorizability and the evaluation of agentic qualities. These findings have significant implications for artificial intelligence systems that learn directly from human interactions.

We present an effective version of Conjecture C (also known as Polymath C), which posits that the repulsion of zeros for automorphic L-functions remains a linear estimate in the degree $d$ generally, and is at least of order $\log N$ in degree specifically. RQL relations are elevated to the language design, enabling the transformation of program-specific invariants into modular specifications. However, distinguishing these relations from trivial constraints is crucial; therefore, this work defines the functional composition of relations together with their metric, establishing a partial order to characterize this composition. Furthermore, we establish strictness criteria that distinguish non-trivial relations from trivial equivalents. Additionally, we present an extension of the original metrical framework through a scalar multiplication operation and a stratified classification system. This design facilitates the manual verification of designated relations within quantum applications and serves as a basis for identifying potential automatisation.

The paper argues that ignoring the fill fraction—the fractional area covered by individual flux tubes—in flux transportation algorithms leads to significant flux tube broadening and inaccurate magnetic field estimates, especially when individual flux measurements are small. A secondary effect involves individual features appearing darker on the photosphere due to radiative transfer changes caused by magnetic fields, an outcome also misrepresented when fill fraction is excluded from inversion. To test this, the author generated synthetic images free from broadening issues using a 3D MHD simulation of a decaying bipolar prominence, which were then used to create two types of comparison images: those created by standard Fefferin-Betzunc (FBR) inversion without fill fraction consideration, and new proposed in-versions that explicitly include it. We demonstrate that while standard FBR results appear reasonable when compared directly to synthetic images, they perform poorly against physically grounded diagnostics such as flux tubes, longitudinal twist, and helicity. Furthermore, a post-processing refinement is developed to enhance the results of maps created without initial inversion for specific features, such as flux tubes. Finally, these findings are applied to analyze a solar bierpolar prominence observed on May 15, 2023, showing significant improvements in the physical realism of maps generated using both existing and new inversion techniques when magnetic fill fraction is explicitly included.

Reverse Adaptive Metropolis (RAMN) algorithms stand as a prominent example of applying Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) methods within control flow normalizing flows (CFNFs). These models infer complex posterior distributions by stacking invertible probability transformations. While prior CV-FF based Monte Carlo simulations showed that these methods can surpass standard Monte Carlo efficiency, there remains a constraint with the normal radial herring transformations used. Despite this, there is no established proof that CV-FF based frameworks are more efficient for these tasks. In this paper, we show significant improvements in a CV-FF framework by utilizing affine coupling layers with complex values. Evidence supports this approach in higher acceptance rates for proposal moves within the chain, along with smaller energy discrepancies during forward and reverse transformations compared to prior work. We also provide theoretical justification explaining these results. Testing across standard benchmarks demonstrates marked performance increases in acceptance rates and posterior estimation accuracy for real-world use cases as well.

Our work introduces ReCross, an innovative unsupervised method for enhancing cross-domain text generation by leveraging high-quality monolithic data for fine-tuning. To counter this, we developed a supervision-free approach that improves upon the initial model tuned with domain-specific high-quality texts. This is achieved by creating synthetic translations of these texts using the same domain, effectively mirating the domain of generation without external supervision. Experiments conducted on machine translation and named entity recognition demonstrate that this technique successfully improves both the generation quality and the overall task performance of neural networks.

Adjusting hyperparameters is essential for achieving peak performance in machine learning models. However, common optimization techniques like grid search are often unfeasible for large-scale or data-intensive tasks, particularly when datasets are private and cannot be transferred externally. Furthermore, simply dividing the hyperparameter grid into groups for parallel Bayesian optimization fails to ensure coverage of the entire search space.

To address these challenges, this paper introduces **Grouped Bayesian Optimization (GBO)**, a group-based methodology designed for distributed environments. Unlike existing group strategies, Grouped Bayesian Acquisitions ensures compatibility across all hyperparameter groups by maintaining consistency in the Bayesian models used within each group through full Bayesian updates.

The approach functions by partitioning the hyperparameter grid into groups, where each group is processed independently and in parallel via Bayesian Optimization. Crucially, this execution can occur entirely within a single local machine, eliminating the need to share data or intermediate results between different nodes.

Our extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of GBO across three distinct machine learning tasks: image generation, new drug discovery, and new drug discovery. These studies demonstrate that individual groups can be solved independently within hours using standard hardware, and the group with the most favorable outcomes yields a model that outperforms those obtained via grid search and group-based sequential Bayesian optimization. Our framework analyzes how initial "precursor features" and "location data" influence the model's output, including rumor reach, peak activity levels, and subsequent decay rates by comparing four distinct scenarios. A one-dimensional thermomechanical model is developed to simulate the quasi-1D behavior of polymers undergoing deformation and crystallization. The theoretical framework incorporates constitutive laws and balance equations for mass, momentum, and energy, solved via a finite difference method. The constitutive approach describes polymers as anisotropic, heterogeneous, and reversible crystallizing materials, accounting for both amorphous and crystalline contributions to stress. These stress components are derived using hyperelasticity theory with specific attention to entropy changes and stress development during the crystallization process. The resulting model is validated against experimental data through numerical simulations of the through-thickness deformation, temperature evolution, and temperature-dependent stress response under various boundary conditions, including fixed temperature and isolated (adiabatic) scenarios. This numerical framework offers a simplified yet practical tool for analyzing the mechanical processes involved in polymer drawing and crystallization.

The original Horodeczki-Lidar-Lloyd (HHL) algorithm and its subsequent adaptations remain untested on actual quantum hardware, primarily because strict polynomial complexity requirements cannot be satisfied on current or near-term platforms where such constraints are relaxed. Recent advances in automatic speech recognition (ASR) have primarily relied on capturing non-linear representations within end-to-end neural networks. However, researchers increasingly recognize the importance of integrating explicit linguistic knowledge and structured prior information to improve performance. Although the incorporation of hand-crafted linguistic features has yielded notable outcomes, proposed mechanisms for encoding these features often remain simplistic and lack effectiveness. Conversely, self-organizing neural architectures inherently generate intricate relationships between speech data and linguistic insights. To address this, we introduce a framework that bidirectionally enhances these existing connections via a novel Bidirectional Attention Mechanism (BiAM). This approach aims to simultaneously refine both the high-level syntactic outputs and the input speech representation, the latter facilitated precisely by the output linguistic attention produced by BiAM. Extensive experiments on the Common Crawl-based ASR corpus demonstrate that compared to current state-of-the-art models, our framework achieves a 1.3 to 1.5 percentage point reduction in character error rate while also producing more accurate generation of ASK (Automated Speech to Text) content.

The critical current of superconducting nanowires is well-established to result from a voltageless state, yet the corresponding critical voltage has long been believed to always originate from a single occupied quasi-particle state. Furthermore, by systematically altering a wire's width and aspect ratio, one can tune the critical voltage so that it either increases or decreases relative to the applied voltage. Collectively, these findings offer novel insights and tools for the design of quantum state metrology devices.

Most real-world AI deployments continue unmodified despite evolving environments, often leading to subpar performance due to concept drift. A primary reason models resist updates is that their initial generalization robustness is frequently mediocre; however, enhancing this can be challenging because traditional methods like additional training on human-labeled data are costly and time-consuming. To offer a more efficient alternative, we introduce DISCO, a method that generates image-text pairs for continuous automatic retraining via natural language instructions. Operating without access to live user interactions, DISCO functions by generating and filtering image captions through the same policy currently in use. It applies this policy to a set of originally trained images to produce a dataset of (text, action) tuples, which are used to update a separate policy network so that it more accurately reflects the current distribution of (text, image) pairs. We demonstrate using a Large Multimodal Model (LMM) that LLMs can achieve greater generalization robustness after just one session of adaptation through data produced by DISCO. Furthermore, this improvement persists even after multiple sessions of adaptation through DISCO, and notably transfers effectively across various language models.

A growth mechanism is proposed where decreasing temperatures enhance the nucleation rate of the $(400)$ domain relative to the $(220)$ domain, yet the $(220)$ facet remains the thermodynamically stable phase under these epitaxial constraints. We present Continuous Information Retrieval Ranking with Label Generation (C2M), a new framework designed to create multi-label dataset labels from existing single-label pairs. Even though having comprehensive data labels offers advantages, obtaining them is frequently costly and time-consuming. Cardiac disease detection is crucial for maintaining public health, yet cardiac electrograms (ECGs) remain largely manual and computationally intensive to analyze using deep methods, often affected by the complexity of heart conditions. This study introduces a novel branch network incorporating attention mechanisms to automatically detect heart disease from electrocardiograms (ECGs). This branch network can effectively concentrate on significant features while eliminating redundant information. The method was tested against the CHAAD dataset to confirm accuracy, and to better reflect actual medical scenarios, all-classes imbalanced and noisy environments were used for assessment. Individual activity recognition (IAR) utilizes data from personal wearables to identify human actions automatically. Although this technology has advanced significantly, most algorithms still rely on large activity datasets annotated with user identities, which is both costly and time-consuming to produce. Federated learning (FL) offers a solution by allowing wearable manufacturers to train models directly on participants' local activity data without accessing it, thereby protecting privacy. However, existing implementations of FL still depend on these expensive labeled public datasets. To address this limitation, we introduce an efficient Federated framework for Wearable-based Health Activity Recognition (FedHealth). This approach employs a one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to extract features directly from raw sensor data and integrates the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to automatically generate labels from unstructured existing datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FedHealth optimizes the overall federated process by utilizing a data sampling strategy that ranks and selects clients based on the efficiency of their contribution. Evaluation results indicate that using unlabeled data with our labeling method yields recognition accuracies comparable to those using fully labeled datasets. Additionally, when working with truly unlabeled data, the method improves FedHealth performance by approximately 7\%.

We demonstrate that standard assumptions regarding Gaussian diffusion can be relaxed when modeling the spread of infectious diseases, specifically showing that simple contact restrictions are capable of producing non-Gaussian distributions of new infections. Specifically, the inclusion of correlations and heterogeneity in infection dynamics independently results in a naturally occurring non-Gaussian distribution of new infections, even if initial conditions are Gaussian. Furthermore, specific contact limitation measures can both induce this non-Gaussian behavior and skew the distribution toward long tails, characterized by more new pandemic cases than typical diffusion predicts. In a general context, these factors and interventions result in a non-Gaussian Gaussian diffusion, preying the model to predict infectious disease outcomes.

GP 2 is our general-purpose Python framework designed to accelerate graph-intensive workloads using GPU accelerators. Established in its first version support for programs involving graphs and multiset collections, it enables efficient handling of large-scale data structures. In this release, we introduce two key advancements: a feature-rich set of graph APIs and a significant performance boost from our newly developed GPU-based BigArray data structure. Six real-world GPU-based Python benchmarks utilizing these enhancements demonstrate an average speedup of 1.9 times compared to the prior version, with specific applications seeing up to 3.5 times faster execution. These improvements were achieved without compromising program generality or requiring manual offloading optimizations.

This work introduces Hierarchical Adversarial Auto-Encoders (HAAE), a unified framework designed to handle both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction and representation learning. For unsupervised extraction, the proposed method employs a hierarchical architecture where hierarchical adversarial constraints are applied exclusively to lower levels of the network. Conversely, the supervised framework utilizes hierarchical auto-encoders; the framework applies label-based constraints in a cascade fashion. At each stage $i$, the system employs a classifier to classify data based on increasingly specific features extracted up to that level, with loss functions backpropagated through the entire model. Theoretical analysis confirms that under appropriate constraints, the features extracted from any layer within this supervised framework achieve zero posterior probability of class labels, a property also observed in similar adversarial frameworks. Extensive experiments validate the method's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches on multiple benchmark datasets for unsupervised feature extraction and feature representation tasks.
